theory.overview: Quantum hardware implementations face the fundamental challenge of maintaining coherent quantum states in a noisy environment. Unlike classical bits that are robust against small perturbations, qubits are extremely sensitive to environmental noise—a problem called decoherence. This chapter explores the leading physical implementations of qubits: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photonics, and neutral atoms. Each has distinct advantages in coherence time, connectivity, gate speed, and scalability. Understanding decoherence mechanisms (T1 energy relaxation and T2 dephasing) is crucial for error correction and algorithm design. Current NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) devices have 10s to 1000s of qubits with gate error rates of 0.1-1%, driving the need for error mitigation and correction strategies.

sections.title: Superconducting Qubits
sections.content: Superconducting circuits are currently the most advanced quantum computing platform, used by IBM, Google, and Rigetti. They use Josephson junctions—nanoscale superconductor-insulator-superconductor sandwiches—to create non-linear inductance. The transmon qubit (transmission-line shunted plasma oscillation) is the most common design, storing quantum information in oscillating current patterns. Pros: fast gates (~10-100 ns), mature fabrication using semiconductor techniques, and natural strong coupling for multi-qubit gates. Cons: millikelvin operating temperatures requiring dilution refrigerators, short coherence times (T1 ~ 100 μs, T2 ~ 100 μs), and sensitivity to charge noise. Recent advances include: tunable couplers for reduced crosstalk, 3D transmons for longer coherence, and processors with 1000+ qubits.

sections.title: Trapped Ion Quantum Computers
sections.content: Trapped ions, pioneered at NIST and used by IonQ and Quantinuum, confine individual atomic ions in electromagnetic traps. Quantum information is stored in internal atomic states (hyperfine or Zeeman sublevels). Laser pulses manipulate qubit states and create entanglement through Coulomb interactions. Pros: extremely high gate fidelities (99.9%+), all-to-all connectivity (any qubit can interact with any other), and identical qubits (no manufacturing variation). Cons: slower gates (~10-100 μs due to motional sideband transitions), complexity of laser systems, and challenges scaling beyond ~50 qubits in a single trap. Modular approaches using ion shuttling between traps may enable larger systems.

sections.title: Photonic Quantum Computing
sections.content: Photonic systems use individual photons as qubits, typically encoding information in polarization, path, or time-bin degrees of freedom. Used by PsiQuantum, Xanadu, and many academic groups. Pros: room temperature operation, natural integration with quantum communication and networking, and photons don't interact with environment (no decoherence during transmission). Cons: deterministic two-qubit gates are difficult (photons don't naturally interact), requiring measurement-based or nonlinear approaches. Probabilistic gates and photon loss are major challenges. Recent progress includes: fusion-based quantum computing for scalability, improved single-photon sources and detectors, and integrated photonic chips for miniaturization.

sections.title: Decoherence: T1 and T2
sections.content: Decoherence is the loss of quantum information due to interaction with the environment. Two primary timescales: T1 (longitudinal relaxation time)—time for excited state |1⟩ to decay to ground state |0⟩, analogous to energy dissipation. T2 (transverse relaxation or dephasing time)—time for quantum superposition to lose phase coherence. T2 is always ≤ 2T1 and often much shorter due to pure dephasing mechanisms. Decoherence limits circuit depth: if gate time is t_g and error rate is ε, maximum operations ~ 1/ε. Current NISQ devices have coherence-limited circuit depths of ~10-1000 gates. Error correction requires physical error rates below ~0.1% and thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit.
sections.circuitDepthLimit: Max gates ≈ min(T₁, T₂) / t_gate × (error threshold)

sections.title: Error Rates and NISQ Era
sections.content: Current quantum devices are in the NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) era: 50-1000+ qubits with noise levels too high for full error correction. Single-qubit gate error rates: 0.01-0.1%. Two-qubit gate error rates: 0.1-1%. Readout errors: 0.5-5%. State-of-the-art systems achieve ~99.9% single-qubit and ~99.5% two-qubit fidelities. Error sources vary by platform: for superconducting qubits—charge noise, flux noise, and materials losses; for trapped ions—laser phase noise and motional heating; for photonics—detector dark counts and source impurity. Error mitigation techniques include: zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation, and symmetry-based verification. True fault-tolerant quantum computing requires logical qubits encoded with quantum error correction codes.
sections.targetForFTQC: Error rates < 0.1% with 1000:1 physical:logical qubit ratio

practiceProblems.title: Coherence Calculation
practiceProblems.description: A superconducting qubit has T₁ = 100 μs and T₂ = 150 μs. What limits the coherence time?
practiceProblems.explanation: T₂ ≤ 2T₁ always. Here T₂ is larger than T₁, so T₁ (energy relaxation) is the limiting factor. However, T₂ specifically measures phase coherence which is often more critical for algorithms.
practiceProblems.hint: Compare T₁ and T₂/2. The smaller value limits coherence.

practiceProblems.title: Gate Count Limit
practiceProblems.description: With T₁ = 100 μs, T₂ = 100 μs, and gate time 50 ns, what's the approximate maximum number of gates before significant decoherence?
practiceProblems.explanation: Number of gates ≈ coherence time / gate time = 100 μs / 50 ns = 100,000 ns / 50 ns = 2000. But with error accumulation, practical limit is ~1000 gates. T₂ being equal to T₁ helps.
practiceProblems.hint: Convert μs to ns: 100 μs = 100,000 ns. Divide by gate time.

practiceProblems.title: Platform Selection
practiceProblems.description: For a quantum algorithm requiring high-fidelity two-qubit gates with all-to-all connectivity, which platform is most suitable?
practiceProblems.explanation: Trapped ions offer all-to-all connectivity and the highest two-qubit gate fidelities (99.9%+). Superconducting qubits typically have nearest-neighbor connectivity. Photonics struggles with deterministic two-qubit gates.
practiceProblems.hint: Consider which platform has both high fidelity and complete connectivity.

codeExample.python:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Decoherence model
def decoherence_model(t, T1, T2, initial_state):
    """
    Model qubit state evolution under decoherence
    initial_state: [alpha, beta] for |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩
    """
    alpha, beta = initial_state
    
    # Population decay (T1 process)
    p1_t = np.abs(beta)**2 * np.exp(-t / T1)
    p0_t = 1 - p1_t
    
    # Coherence decay (T2 process)
    coherence = alpha * np.conj(beta) * np.exp(-t / T2)
    
    return p0_t, p1_t, np.abs(coherence)

# Parameters
T1 = 100e-6  # 100 microseconds
T2 = 80e-6   # 80 microseconds (T2 < T1 is common)
t_gate = 50e-9  # 50 nanosecond gates

# Time array
t = np.linspace(0, 5*T1, 1000)

# Initial state |+⟩
initial = [1/np.sqrt(2), 1/np.sqrt(2)]

# Calculate decoherence
p0, p1, coherence = decoherence_model(t, T1, T2, initial)

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.semilogy(t * 1e6, p1, label='P(|1⟩) - Population', linewidth=2)
plt.semilogy(t * 1e6, coherence, label='|ρ₀₁| - Coherence', linewidth=2)
plt.axhline(y=1/np.e, color='r', linestyle='--', label='1/e threshold')
plt.xlabel('Time (μs)')
plt.ylabel('Probability / Coherence')
plt.title('Qubit Decoherence: T₁ = 100μs, T₂ = 80μs')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

print(f"Max gates (theoretical): {int(T2 / t_gate)}")
print(f"Population at T₁: {np.exp(-1):.3f}")
print(f"Coherence at T₂: {np.exp(-1):.3f}")
